lesson.title: Days, Months & Dates
lesson.subtitle: maandag, januari, vandaag — the calendar words English and Dutch share

hook.title: The Calendar Is Almost Free
hook.content: Maandag, dinsdag, januari: the calendar is a museum of shared loans and shared Germanic gods. The only new work is the little prepositions that tell you when.

pattern.title: Day, month, preposition
pattern.content: Op maandag ('on Monday'), in januari ('in January'), vandaag, morgen, gisteren. Dutch uses op for days, in for months, and the time words stand alone.
pattern.trap_note: Do not use op before a month or in before a day. The preposition follows the unit of time.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Days, Months & Dates):
exercises.target_answer: de maandag, de dinsdag, de januari, vandaag, de morgen, gisteren
exercises.meaning: Monday, Tuesday, January, today, tomorrow; morning, yesterday
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Days, Months & Dates": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Vandaag is het maandag.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Days, Months & Dates”.
“Morgen is het dinsdag.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Day, month, preposition.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not use op before a month or in before a day. The preposition follows the unit of time.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
options: not In January is it cold.
exercises.explanation: “In januari is het koud.” is word-for-word “In January is it cold.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Day, month, preposition.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: On Monday I work.
exercises.explanation: “Op maandag werk ik.” reuses only material taught in “Days, Months & Dates” — Day, month, preposition.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Op maandag werk ik.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Day, month, preposition.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “Today is Wednesday.”
twist.explanation: The same frame as the other days; only the day name changes.

summary.outcome: Name days and months, and choose op or in for dates.
summary.takeaway: Calendar vocabulary is a loan; calendar grammar is a preposition choice.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Calendar Gym.

maandag.etymology_derivation: A day named for the moon, like English Monday.

dinsdag.etymology_derivation: A day named for an old Germanic god, like English Tuesday.

januari.etymology_derivation: The same Latin month name as English January.

vandaag.etymology_derivation: van ('of') + dag ('day'): on the day of today.

morgen.etymology_derivation: English morrow and Dutch morgen are the same word.

gisteren.etymology_derivation: English yesterday and Dutch gisteren are the same time word.
